vendor_011:n1.prompt:
You are helping me define requirements and constraints for selecting an AI assistant ({{vendor}}) to support knowledge-work tasks like document/presentation creation and organizing project context. This is step one of a vendor selection process (requirements → shortlist → comparison → trial → security review → negotiation), so your output here will feed later research and evaluation steps.

If you don't already know it, ask me for: (1) my domain/industry and team size, (2) the specific knowledge-work tasks I need supported (e.g., drafting docs, building presentations, editing exportable files), (3) my current software stack (docs, storage, chat/collab tools) the assistant must fit alongside, (4) any compliance, data residency, or security constraints, (5) budget range and number of seats needed, (6) must-have vs nice-to-have features.

Using my answers, produce a structured requirements document covering:
- Functional requirements: ability to create and iteratively edit documents, presentations, and other files with export support; ability to organize related chats and files into a shared project/space with persistent context and instructions; any other workflow needs I specify.
- Non-functional requirements: security/compliance constraints, integration needs with my existing stack, performance/reliability expectations.
- Constraints: budget ceiling, seat count, deployment timeline, any vendors or approaches to exclude.
- Success criteria: how I'll know a candidate meets my needs (e.g., can produce an exportable deck from a prompt, can maintain context across a multi-file project).

Format the output as a clear markdown document with labeled sections (Functional Requirements, Non-Functional Requirements, Constraints, Success Criteria) so it can be handed directly to the next step (market research and shortlisting). Do not research or name specific products yet — this step is requirements-only. Report back with the completed requirements document and a short list of any open questions I still need to answer before shortlisting can begin.

vendor_011:n2.prompt:
You are helping me research and shortlist vendors in the "ai-assistants" market (products like {{vendor}}) as candidates for a function we need to support. Before starting, ask me for: (1) the specific task/function this assistant must perform, (2) our current software stack it needs to fit with, (3) any must-have requirements or constraints I already have (budget, security posture, integrations), and (4) how many candidates I want shortlisted (default to 4-6 if I don't specify).

Once you have this, use web research (and, if available, browser-operating or deep-research capabilities) to identify products in the ai-assistants market that plausibly fit our stated requirements. For each candidate, gather and cite evidence on: whether it can operate a web browser autonomously to complete multi-step tasks, whether it supports launching a deep research run that searches many sources and returns a cited report, and whether it can answer questions grounded in current web results with source citations. Note pricing tier, deployment model, and any obvious compatibility notes with our current stack.

Produce a shortlist as a table: vendor name (using {{vendor}} as placeholder where a specific product name would go, since I will substitute my chosen vendor), key capabilities matched against the three criteria above, stack-fit notes, pricing signal, and a source citation/link for each claim.

Done looks like: a written shortlist of 4-6 candidates with evidence-backed comparisons ready for me to review, plus a short summary of which 2-3 look strongest given my stated requirements and why. Do not sign up for trials, submit forms, or make purchasing decisions — this step is research only. Report back with the shortlist table, your top recommendations, and any open questions you need me to answer before we move to detailed comparison and trials.

For any research based solely on public web information without a specific vendor market action, proceed directly since this step is research-only and requires no sign-off.

vendor_011:n3.prompt:
You are helping me compare shortlisted software candidates for a specific function against my existing stack, using judged evidence, and produce a ranked recommendation. If you don't already have them, ask me for: (1) the function this software is for, (2) the shortlist of candidate products/services (by actual name), (3) the requirements and evaluation criteria defined earlier in this process, and (4) a list of the tools, platforms, and systems in my current stack that the new software must integrate with or fit alongside.

Once you have this, for each candidate: research publicly available evidence (docs, changelogs, pricing pages, integration lists, security/compliance pages, independent reviews, benchmark or case-study data) to assess how well it meets each requirement. Explicitly check compatibility with each item in my current stack (data formats, APIs, auth methods, hosting model, language/framework support, etc.) and flag any gaps, extra middleware needed, or migration effort. Note evidence quality (official docs vs. marketing claims vs. third-party review) for each finding so I can judge reliability.

Produce a comparison table scoring each candidate against every requirement and stack-compatibility check, with a short evidence citation or note per score. Follow with a ranked list (best fit to worst) and a one-paragraph rationale per candidate explaining strengths, weaknesses, and stack-fit risks.

Done looks like: a clear ranked table plus written rationale for every shortlisted candidate, all major claims backed by cited sources, and explicit flags on any stack-compatibility risks or unknowns still needing verification.

Report back with the full comparison table, the ranking, the rationale summaries, and a list of any open questions or evidence gaps I should resolve before moving to trials.

vendor_011:n4.prompt:
You are helping me run hands-on agentic trials of the top candidate software options I've shortlisted for a specific function in my stack. Before starting, ask me for anything missing: (1) the function/task this software must perform, (2) the names of the 2-3 shortlisted candidate products/services (use their real names, not placeholders), (3) my current tech stack and any systems the new tool must integrate with, (4) the key requirements/acceptance criteria defined earlier (must-haves, nice-to-haves, performance thresholds), and (5) confirmation that trial/sandbox accounts exist or need creating using my configured credentials.

For each candidate: sign in or set up the trial environment, then design and run realistic test scenarios that exercise the core requirements against my existing stack — e.g., data import/export, API or integration behavior, automation workflows, error handling, and edge cases relevant to my use case. Log objective, judged evidence for each: accuracy/output quality, latency, reliability, cost implications at expected usage, ease of integration with my current tools, and any friction, bugs, or missing features encountered during the trial.

After trials, produce a structured comparison document scoring each candidate against the requirements, with concrete evidence (not opinions) supporting each score, plus a short list of open questions or risks to raise before security review and negotiation.

Done looks like: each candidate has been actually exercised end-to-end (not just read about), a comparison scorecard exists with evidence-backed ratings, and a clear leader (or tie) emerges with rationale.

Report back with: the comparison scorecard, key findings per candidate, any blockers or unresolved risks, and your recommended next candidate(s) to carry into security review.

vendor_011:n5.prompt:
You are helping me complete a security and data review for a software vendor I'm considering onboarding. If you don't already know it, ask me for: (1) the vendor's name, (2) the function/data it will handle, (3) links or access to their SOC2 report, Data Processing Agreement (DPA), and any security questionnaire or trust center page, and (4) our internal compliance requirements or checklist if one exists (e.g., required certifications, data residency rules, breach notification SLAs).

Then do the following:
1. Pull and read the vendor's SOC2 report (Type I or II), DPA, and any published security documentation or trust center content.
2. Summarize their data handling practices: what data they store/process, encryption at rest and in transit, subprocessor list, data retention and deletion policies, and data residency.
3. Note their compliance certifications (SOC2, ISO 27001, HIPAA, GDPR readiness, etc.) and flag any gaps, exclusions, or exceptions in the audit report.
4. Research and summarize any known breach history or public security incidents involving this vendor.
5. Compare the DPA terms against standard requirements (liability caps, breach notification timelines, audit rights, sub-processor approval) and flag any unusual or concerning clauses.
6. Produce a single structured summary document with sections: Data Handling, Certifications & Gaps, Breach History, DPA Concerns, and an overall risk flag (low/medium/high) with reasoning.

Do not make any acceptance, approval, or onboarding decision yourself. This requires judgment from someone with security authority, so once your summary is ready, stop for human sign-off. Report back with the summary document and a short list of open questions or risks that need explicit human judgment before proceeding.

vendor_011:n6.prompt:
You are helping me prepare for a vendor pricing/terms negotiation. I have selected a finalist vendor after trial and security review. Ask me for anything you need that's missing: the vendor's name, the product/service being purchased, the proposed pricing quote or contract draft I've received, my current spend on comparable tools, my budget ceiling, expected usage volume/seat count, contract term length preferences, and any must-have terms (e.g. data residency, SLA, cancellation rights, auto-renewal caps).

Once you have this context, please:
1. Summarize the vendor's current offer in a clear table (price, term length, payment schedule, key contract clauses).
2. Research and list typical market benchmarks or public pricing tiers for this category of service, if available, to give me leverage context.
3. Draft a counter-proposal document with specific asks (e.g., discount %, multi-year lock-in trade, added support tier, liability caps, exit clauses) framed as talking points I can send or say to the vendor's sales rep.
4. Prepare a comparison sheet showing 'their offer' vs 'my counter' vs 'walk-away threshold' so I can see tradeoffs at a glance.
5. Flag any contract terms that look risky or nonstandard (auto-renewal, unilateral price increases, data ownership) for my review.

Do not contact the vendor, send emails, submit forms, or agree to any terms yourself — the actual back-and-forth negotiation and final terms decision remains a human step. Your job is only to prepare drafts, benchmarks, and comparison materials.

When finished, report back with: the offer summary, the draft counter-proposal, the comparison sheet, and the list of flagged risky terms, then stop for human sign-off before any negotiation communication is sent or terms are accepted.

vendor_011:n7.prompt:
You are helping me prepare the final negotiated agreement for e-signature using {{vendor}}, our chosen legal-ops platform. Before starting, ask me for: (1) the finalized agreement text or template name, (2) the list of signatories with names, roles, and email addresses, (3) any custom fields (dates, dollar amounts, party names) that need to be populated, and (4) confirmation of my {{vendor}} account access (use your configured credentials).

Once you have these, do the following: create a new document set or envelope from the appropriate template in {{vendor}}, populate all required fields with the negotiated terms I provide, and render or preview the forms so I can confirm every value is correct before anything is sent. Set up the signer routing order exactly as I specify (e.g., counterparty first, then our authorized signer), and stage the document for signature but do NOT send it yet.

Produce a summary for me showing: the document set/envelope name or ID, all populated field values, the signer list with routing order, and a link or reference to review the staged document inside {{vendor}}. Flag any missing or ambiguous fields that need my input before this can go out.

This step requires my explicit approval before the agreement is dispatched for signature, so once everything is staged and summarized, stop for human sign-off. Do not click send, submit, or finalize the signature request yourself — wait for me to review and explicitly approve before you (or I) trigger the actual send action.

vendor_011:n8.prompt:
You are helping me finalize the signature step for our vendor agreement with n8n (workflow automation software) after negotiation is complete. Please do the following:

1. Ask me for: (a) the final negotiated contract/order form (PDF or link), (b) the legal name and title of our authorized signatory, (c) our company's legal entity name and billing address, (d) which e-signature platform will be used (e.g., DocuSign, PandaDoc, or the vendor's own portal), and (e) any redlines or side-letter terms we agreed to during negotiation that must appear in the final document.

2. Review the final contract text against the negotiated terms I provide, and flag any discrepancies in pricing, contract term/renewal, SLA commitments, data processing/DPA terms, termination clauses, or liability caps.

3. Prepare a one-page internal summary of key contract terms (price, term length, auto-renewal date, cancellation notice period, data handling terms) for our records and for the signatory's quick reference.

4. If an e-signature tool is being used, pre-fill the signer's name, title, email, and company details in the send/prepare screen, and attach the correct final contract version — but do not click send, sign, approve, or submit the agreement yourself.

5. Produce a short checklist for the signatory confirming: contract matches negotiated terms, summary reviewed, and any open questions resolved.

Only an authorized officer may legally bind the company to this contract, so once everything is drafted, prepared, and verified, stop for human sign-off — do not sign, accept terms, approve, or submit the agreement on my behalf.

Report back with: the discrepancy list (if any), the key-terms summary, confirmation that the e-signature draft is ready for review, and the checklist for the signatory.

vendor_011:n9.prompt:
You are helping me connect and roll out a newly selected software vendor to my team. This follows vendor selection, security review, and a signed agreement, so assume procurement is done — this step is purely technical setup and team enablement.

Before starting, ask me for anything missing: (1) the name of the vendor/software we selected, (2) the function or workflow it serves, (3) the list of team members (names/emails) who need access, (4) how we currently manage identity (e.g., our SSO/identity provider or directory), (5) any existing tools in our stack it needs to integrate with (e.g., Slack, GitHub, our CRM), and (6) whether this is a standard SaaS connection or an MCP server connection.

Then do the following: log in using my configured credentials; configure authentication/single sign-on for the vendor using our existing identity provider if supported; create any required DNS records or configuration settings via the vendor's dashboard or API, describing each step in plain language rather than raw commands; connect the vendor to the other tools in our stack it needs to talk to; invite each team member and assign appropriate roles/permissions based on their function; verify connectivity end-to-end (e.g., test login, test a core workflow action) and confirm data flows correctly between systems; and document the final configuration, including who has access, what integrations are live, and any settings changed.

Done looks like: every listed team member has working access with correct permissions, all required integrations are connected and verified, and configuration is documented.

Report back with: a summary of what was connected, a table of team members and their access levels, confirmation of successful verification tests, and any issues or manual follow-ups needed.
